reads.name: portal.summary
reads.why: The portal's front page. Aggregates over contracts, which is 98,636 rows and the largest table anyone reaches through a browser.

reads.name: portal.contracts.first_page
reads.why: The contracts list as it first loads, ordered by date_published — which no index covers today, and is candidate one for Phase 4 index work.

reads.name: portal.contracts.full_page
reads.why: The same list at its cap. The plan expected the portal to paginate with OFFSET and it does not — `contracts()` takes a limit and no offset, and the cap is what protects it — so the deep-OFFSET cost the keyset-pagination proposal is aimed at lives on the admin side only, below. This is what the portal's worst case actually is.

reads.name: portal.geography
reads.why: The map's payload: grant totals per authority, joined across the authority spine.

reads.name: portal.authority
reads.why: The heaviest payload the portal serves: one authority's grant, budget, treatment and contracts, composed from the same functions the individual pages use.

reads.name: portal.layers
reads.why: The map's layer index, including a coverage count per authority over every evidence table.

reads.name: portal.boundaries
reads.why: 347 generalised boundary polygons. Dominated by moving text rather than by the query, which is worth knowing before anyone optimises the query.

reads.name: portal.providers
reads.why: Goes through v_provider_viability, the view whose bare GROUP BY had to be restructured for PostgreSQL. If the rewrite cost anything, it shows up here.

reads.name: portal.pay
reads.why: Includes _median_value, which loads every priced notice into Python and sorts it there. percentile_cont is the Phase 4 replacement, and this is what it has to beat.

reads.name: portal.fingertips
reads.why: 22,667 rows behind a view, filtered per indicator.

reads.name: portal.authorities
reads.why: ORDER BY name over the authority spine — the query whose answer changes if the collation is wrong.

reads.name: admin.read_table.contracts
reads.why: The table browser on the biggest table, in primary-key order — what replaced ORDER BY rowid.

reads.name: admin.read_table.budgets_deep
reads.why: 477,199 rows, paged near the end. The worst OFFSET in the application.

reads.name: admin.read_table.search
reads.why: LIKE with an escaped term over every column cast to text. Case sensitivity differs between the engines and the cost does too.

reads.name: admin.review_items
reads.why: The operator's worklist, ordered by created_at and id — already the sort keyset pagination would use.

reads.name: admin.review_items.deep_offset
reads.why: The same worklist near the end of 4,822 items. This and the budgets page below are the two numbers that decide whether Phase 4's keyset pagination is worth building.

reads.name: admin.list_objects
reads.why: Sidebar, on every page load of the operator UI. One COUNT(*) per table until Phase 4 — 82 of them, which is 82 round-trips over a LAN — and one statement since.

reads.name: admin.health.freshness
reads.why: Deliberately unindexed full scans of every table carrying retrieved_at. Documented as expensive on purpose; the question is how expensive, on each engine.
